blocks.content: Your model scores 99 percent on training data. You show the numbers around. Production accuracy drops to 62 percent. Nothing broke. The model learned the wrong lesson. Welcome to overfitting. Every data science student hits this wall. A notebook full of perfect scores turns into a project nobody trusts. The gap has a name, a cause, and a set of fixes you will reuse for years.

An overfitted model memorizes training examples instead of learning the patterns behind them. Training data always carries noise. Typos in labels. One-off coincidences. Outliers from a bad sensor. A model with enough capacity treats every quirk as a rule. Training accuracy climbs toward 100 percent. New data tells a different story.

An underfitted model never picks up the pattern at all. A straight line drawn through curved data misses the shape completely. Both scores stay low. Training score. Test score. No memorization happened. No learning happened either. Underfitting usually means the model was too simple for the problem.

blocks.text: The bias-variance tradeoff, in plain words

blocks.content: Bias means a model oversimplifies. A high-bias model bends every problem toward the same shape, no matter what the data says. Variance means a model overreacts. A high-variance model redraws its answers around every data point, including the noisy ones. Simple models lean toward high bias. Complex models lean toward high variance. Good models land somewhere in between. Memorize one sentence for interviews. Bias is error from wrong assumptions. Variance is error from sensitivity to noise.

Split your data before training. Train on one part. Hold out another part for testing. Compare the two scores. A wide gap points to overfitting. This loop shows the gap growing as a decision tree gets deeper.

blocks.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=42)

for depth in [1, 3, 5, 10, None]:
    model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=42)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    train_score = model.score(X_train, y_train)
    test_score = model.score(X_test, y_test)
    print(f"depth={depth} train={train_score:.3f} test={test_score:.3f}")

# depth=1    train=0.923 test=0.895
# depth=3    train=0.972 test=0.958
# depth=5    train=0.995 test=0.958
# depth=10   train=1.000 test=0.951
# depth=None train=1.000 test=0.951

blocks.content: Depth 3 gives the best balance here. Past this point, training accuracy keeps climbing while test accuracy slides. The model stops learning the disease pattern and starts memorizing individual patients.
1. Add more training data. Extra examples smooth out noise. Memorizing gets harder when examples multiply.
2. Simplify the model. Limit tree depth. Drop weak features. Fewer moving parts means less room for memorization.

3. Regularize. Regularization penalizes large weights, which forces the model to prefer simple explanations. RidgeClassifier applies an L2 penalty controlled by alpha. A small alpha means a light penalty. A large alpha means a heavy penalty. Watch the scores shift as alpha changes.

blocks.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)

for alpha in [0.01, 1.0, 100.0]:
    model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), RidgeClassifier(alpha=alpha))
    scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)
    print(f"alpha={alpha} mean={scores.mean():.3f}")

# alpha=0.01  mean=0.960
# alpha=1.0   mean=0.958
# alpha=100.0 mean=0.949

blocks.content: Always scale features before training regularized models. Without scaling, features with large values dominate the penalty for no good reason.
4. Stop training early. Neural networks and gradient boosting improve for a while, then start memorizing. Track validation loss after each round. Stop when the loss starts rising.
5. Cross-validate. A single train-test split depends on luck. Five-fold cross-validation trains and tests five times on different slices, then averages. The average tells a steadier story.

Underfitting fixes point the other way. Add richer features. Try polynomial terms. Let trees grow deeper. Train for more epochs. Scale features so gradient-based models update evenly. When both scores stay low together, the model needs more room, not less. Read the score pair like a dashboard. Low train plus low test means underfitting. High train plus low test means overfitting. High train plus high test means you are done.

Take any classifier on any dataset you own. Run the depth loop from the first code block. Find the depth where test accuracy peaks. Now run the same loop with min_samples_leaf set to 20. Notice how the peak moves. Two runs, one insight, and a pattern you will repeat on every project.

blocks.text: A model with perfect training accuracy is bragging about its memory. Real skill shows on data the model has never seen.

title: Overfitting: Why Models Memorize Instead of Learning
